Concentration of a total across units

Source: R/concentration.R
concentration.Rd

Measures how unevenly a total is spread across units: whether a few people account for most of the placements, or a few regions for most of the days. ginicoef() gives the Gini coefficient, lorenzc() the points of the Lorenz curve (for plotting, for example with plotlrnz()), and topshr() the share of the total held by the largest units (“the top 1% of people account for 20% of the days”). The three are computed in compiled code from the same sorted values.

Usage

ginicoef(x, na.rm = TRUE)

lorenzc(x, na.rm = TRUE)

topshr(x, fracs = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25), na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of non-negative values, one per unit (for example the days or the count of placements of each person). NA values are dropped; Inf, negative values and non-numeric input are errors.

na.rm

Logical. Missing values are dropped whatever its value; the argument exists so the call reads the same as base R's. Default TRUE.

fracs

Numeric vector of fractions of the units, each in [0, 1]: for each one the share of the total held by that fraction of units, taking the largest units first. Default c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25).

Value

ginicoef(): a numeric scalar in [0, 1 - 1/n]. lorenzc(): a data frame with numeric columns population (cumulative share of units, from 0 to 1) and value (cumulative share of the total, units in ascending order), n + 1 rows including the origin. topshr(): a data frame with columns fraction (the requested fraction of units), units (how many of the largest units that fraction is) and share (the share of the total those units hold).

Details

Gini is the mean absolute difference between pairs of units over twice the mean, \(G = \sum_i \sum_j |x_i - x_j| / (2 n^2 \bar{x})\), which is also twice the area between the Lorenz curve and the diagonal. Zero is a perfectly even spread; the maximum for n units is 1 - 1/n, not 1, so a Gini near 1 requires many units as well as an uneven spread.

A Gini computed from banded or rounded data inherits that coarsening: compare with bandsens() when the values are bands. For a tail that a few units dominate, hilltlidx() says whether the largest values follow a power law.

Errors: x not numeric, with Inf or a negative value, or with no non-missing value; ginicoef() when every value is zero (the Gini of a zero total is undefined); topshr() when fractions is not numeric, is empty, has NA or lies outside [0, 1].

References

Hedderich, J. and Sachs, L. (2020). Applied Statistics: Methods Using R. Springer-Verlag, Berlin Heidelberg. Section 3.14, p. 117, gives the construction used here: the units are placed at equal intervals on the horizontal axis and the cumulated, ascendingly ordered shares of the total on the vertical one, so that the curve is the diagonal exactly when p percent of the units account for p percent of the total, and sags further the greater the concentration.

See also

hilltlidx(), bandsens()

Examples

# Ten units holding one each: no concentration.
ginicoef(rep(1, 10))
#> [1] 0

# One unit holding everything: the maximum for ten units.
ginicoef(c(rep(0, 9), 1))
#> [1] 0.9
1 - 1 / 10
#> [1] 0.9

placements <- c(rep(1, 1200), rep(3, 430), rep(8, 110), rep(20, 38))
ginicoef(placements)
#> [1] 0.461225

# What the most frequent few account for.
topshr(placements, c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1))
#>   fraction units      share
#> 1     0.01    18 0.08716707
#> 2     0.05    89 0.28280872
#> 3     0.10   178 0.41888620

head(lorenzc(placements))
#>     population        value
#> 1 0.0000000000 0.0000000000
#> 2 0.0005624297 0.0002421308
#> 3 0.0011248594 0.0004842615
#> 4 0.0016872891 0.0007263923
#> 5 0.0022497188 0.0009685230
#> 6 0.0028121485 0.0012106538

# missing values are dropped
ginicoef(c(1, NA, 3))
#> [1] 0.25

# a zero total has no Gini coefficient
try(ginicoef(c(0, 0, 0)))
#> Error : every value is zero: the Gini coefficient of a zero total is undefined
